content_units: Knee Pain After Starting Daily Walks

Based on what you described, this most often fits an   overuse problem around the kneecap   rather than an infection or major injury. Pain that is   around the kneecap   and   worse going downstairs   commonly points to irritation in the   patellofemoral joint   or nearby soft tissues.
Brief context

This is general information, not a diagnosis. The combination of   age 67  ,   new daily walks  ,   3 weeks of mild pain  ,   no swelling  ,   no fever  ,   no injury  , and   still able to walk   makes a serious emergency cause less likely, but persistent pain still deserves monitoring.
Likely Causes of Front-of-Knee Pain
Possible cause   Why it fits   Typical clues
Patellofemoral pain   Very common with pain around the kneecap and worse with stairs, especially downstairs   Ache behind/around kneecap; worse after walking hills, stairs, or sitting long periods
Flare of knee osteoarthritis   Common at his age; walking increase can irritate the joint   Activity-related pain, stiffness after rest, crunching/grinding, gradual onset
Patellar tendon or quadriceps tendon irritation   Can happen after increasing walking volume or hills   Pain just below or above kneecap; worse with stairs or repeated bending
Mild cartilage irritation/overload   New repetitive activity can temporarily overload the kneecap joint   Pain with squatting, stairs, longer walks, or getting up from a chair
Home Care for the Next 1–2 Weeks
-   Reduce walking temporarily  , rather than stopping all movement completely.
- Try   shorter, flatter walks   every other day for several days, then increase slowly if pain is settling.
- Use   ice for 15–20 minutes   after walks, 3–5 times a day if helpful.
- If stiff more than sore, some people prefer   gentle heat before activity   and ice after.
- Encourage   supportive walking shoes   with good cushioning.
- Avoid deep knee bending when possible for now.
- If comfortable, he can try   gentle range-of-motion  :
- slow knee bends within a pain-free range
- straight-leg raises
- gentle calf and hamstring stretching
- A   simple knee sleeve   may help some people feel more supported, though it does not treat the cause.
Pain relief note

Because he is   allergic to ibuprofen   and takes   blood pressure medication  , it is safest   not to assume other anti-inflammatory medicines are okay   without checking with a clinician or pharmacist.
Options that are often considered safer for some people include:
-   Acetaminophen/paracetamol  , if he normally can take it and follows label dosing
- A   topical pain-relief product   may be considered, but because of the ibuprofen allergy, he should confirm with a pharmacist before using any   NSAID gel   such as diclofenac
What to Avoid Right Now
Option 1: Long walks at his new full distance   Most likely trigger if this started after increasing activity   Reduce duration/frequency first
Option 2: Downhill walking and repeated stairs   These load the kneecap joint more heavily   Limit for 1–2 weeks if possible
Option 3: Deep squats, lunges, kneeling   Often worsen kneecap pain   Avoid until pain clearly improves
Option 4: “Push through the pain” exercise   Can prolong irritation   Keep activity at a mild, tolerable level
When a Prompt Medical Appointment Is Justified
A   prompt appointment in the next day or few days   is reasonable if any of these happen:
- Pain is   getting worse instead of better
- He develops   swelling  , warmth, or visible redness
- The knee   gives way  , locks, or he cannot bend/straighten it normally
- Walking becomes clearly more difficult or he starts limping a lot
- Pain begins to disturb sleep regularly
- Symptoms last   more than a few weeks despite reducing activity
- He has significant morning stiffness or pain in multiple joints
- He wants medication advice because of   blood pressure treatment   and   ibuprofen allergy
Seek urgent care sooner if:
-   Fever   develops with knee pain
- The calf becomes swollen or painful
- He suddenly cannot bear weight
- There is major swelling after even a minor twist or misstep
- The knee becomes markedly red, hot, or severely painful
